title: The $100 Lens Sanduk Ruit Set Out to Make for $4 in Kathmandu
dek: In 1994 a Nepali eye surgeon opened his own centre outside government and set about manufacturing cataract lenses his patients could afford.

story.event: Opening Tilganga outside government and building a lens factory to make cataract lenses affordable
story.summary: In 1994 Sanduk Ruit opened the Tilganga Eye Centre in Kathmandu, choosing an independent institution over the government system, to offer cataract surgery with implanted lenses that then cost about $100 each. With the Fred Hollows Foundation he set out to make the lenses in Nepal; a first attempt failed and a new process took until 1996. By 2006 Tilganga had supplied nearly 1.5 million lenses to some fifty countries for under $5 each.
paragraphs: In the early 1980s Sanduk Ruit, a young Nepali doctor from a remote mountain village, worked on Nepal's first national blindness survey. What he saw troubled him. Cataract surgery, as then practised, removed the clouded lens and left patients with thick, heavy glasses. Many gave them up, he later said, so surgeons were "virtually leaving the patients functionally blind." The modern alternative, an implanted plastic lens, cost about $100, far beyond most of his patients.

Through that work he met the Australian ophthalmologist Fred Hollows, and after training with him Ruit was implanting lenses in Nepal by 1988. Local eye surgeons resisted; he patiently taught them and began to win converts, and he carried the surgery to remote eye camps, devising a stitch-free technique on the way.

By his own account he then wanted an institution with flexible management, free of the bureaucratic hurdles of government hospitals. In 1994 he opened the Tilganga Eye Centre in Kathmandu, founded, the Kathmandu Post later reported, with five others and $200. A local trust donated the land, local people and organisations paid for the building, and an Australian group, the Nepal Eye Programme, covered running costs for a year. The new centre, he said, disturbed people established in the trade, and someone tried to vandalise it. The other decision was to make the lenses in Nepal rather than import them. Hollows had laid plans for lens factories in Nepal and Eritrea, but died of cancer before Tilganga or its laboratory opened.

The first attempt failed. Working with the Fred Hollows Foundation, Ruit said, the team began on an older version of the lens that did not work out; developing a new process took from 1994 to 1996, after which they built a team of Nepali scientists to run it. A 2018 press release from the charity of Ray Avery, the scientist who built the factory, said surgeons at first would not buy lenses made in Nepal until an independent expert vouched for them. By 2006, the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation reported, Tilganga had supplied nearly 1.5 million lenses to some fifty countries for under $5 each; Ruit put the cost at $4. Surgery was priced by ability to pay, and the poor paid nothing.

quote.text: It is another that attaineth by giving unto him that hath not; not he that causeth men dread.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Ptahhotep says the one who truly gains is the one who gives to those who have nothing, not the one who rules by fear. Tilganga began on donated land and gifts, charged the poor nothing, and by 2006, Ruit said, paid its own way.

reflection: Ruit's lens did not begin as a triumph. The first version did not work, the process took two years to get right, and, according to the factory's builder, surgeons at first would not trust a lens made in Nepal. What drove it, in his own telling, was plain arithmetic: a $100 lens was of no use to patients who could not pay for it.

You will know versions of that arithmetic, in the price of kits and equipment that arrive from far away. Not every one of them can be made nearer home, and that is no failing. But now and then it is worth asking which things you treat as fixed only look fixed because nobody close by has tried yet.
invitation: Pick one cost or supply in your work that everyone treats as fixed. Ask one colleague today what it would take to source or make it nearer, and simply note the answer.

cross_checks.claim: Ruit opened the Tilganga Eye Centre in Kathmandu in 1994
Tilganga made lenses for about US$4 when imported lenses cost about US$100
After training with Hollows, Ruit was introducing lens implant surgery in Nepal by 1988
Hollows died before Tilganga and its lens laboratory opened
The first lens-making effort did not work out

research_notes: Lens prices differ: Ruit (Down To Earth 2006, his Magsaysay response) and The Himalayan Times give about US$100 for an imported lens and US$4 for Tilganga's; the Magsaysay citation says under US$5; Nepali Times (2012) says US$150 before; a Himalayan Cataract Project nomination on the IAPB site says US$200 to US$4; the Kathmandu Post (2018) says US$3 against over US$100. The story uses Ruit's own US$100 and US$4, and the citation's 'under $5'. Founding year: 1994 in the Magsaysay citation, Nepali Times, the Fred Hollows Foundation and Ruit's interview; the IAPB nomination says Ruit founded a Tilganga eye clinic in 1992 (not cited); the story uses 1994. Lens totals rise over time and are not mixed: nearly 1.5 million by 2006 (Magsaysay; Nepali Times 2006), three million by 2012 (Nepali Times), five million people by 2018 (Avery's press release); only the 2006 figure is used. When Ruit and Hollows met is dated variously (survey of 1980 or 1981; Hollows's 1985 WHO visit in the Kathmandu Post), so no date is given. Ruit's account of the first, failed lens attempt (an 'older version of intra-ocular lens') is paraphrased; Avery's charity says the original equipment did not work and buyers were reluctant, which is attributed to the press release because it is a self-interested source. The 'five others and $200' detail is the Kathmandu Post's statement, not a direct quotation. The vandalism is Ruit's own claim, without detail. Hollows died in 1993 according to general references, but the cited sources say only that he died before Tilganga and the laboratory opened, so no year is given. Down To Earth gives the land donor as the 'Pashupati Development Trust'; the story says 'a local trust'. The centre is now called the Tilganga Institute of Ophthalmology; the company field uses the 1994 name only, because the words of the later name matched unrelated institutions in the repeat screen. The screen still flags Aravind Eye Hospital (Venkataswamy, India, 1976) on the shared word "Eye"; it is a different founder, country and episode.
